topic: The lion and the clever rabbit
outline:
In a green forest, a proud old lion demands that one animal come to him every day.
The animals are frightened and agree to take turns to go to the lion.
One day it is the turn of a tiny but clever rabbit to go.
The rabbit walks slowly and arrives late, thinking of a clever plan.
The rabbit tells the lion, another lion in the forest says he is the real king.
The angry lion roars and asks to be taken to this other lion at once.
The rabbit leads him to a deep old well and shows him a lion face in the water below.
The lion roars at his own reflection, slips into the water with a splash, and the forest animals are safe at last.
check: Made gentle: Softened for ages 3-9: no killing or eating is shown; the lion only demands and frightens. The traditional drowning is softened to a splash into the well and the animals becoming safe, with the lion humbled rather than harmed.

source: Tenali Rama folk tales, Telugu tradition of Andhra Pradesh
outline:
Tenali Rama lives with his wife in a small house in Vijayanagara.
Late one night he hears quiet whispers and footsteps on the roof.
He understands thieves have come to steal, and whispers his plan to his wife.
Loudly so the thieves can hear, he says to throw all their valuables in a box into the garden well for safety.
His wife drops a big heavy box with only stones and old pots into the well with a loud splash.
The thieves climb down into the well to find the treasure box.
Tenali Rama calls down kindly and asks them to pass up buckets of water to water his garden plants, and they work all night while he sings.
At sunrise the tired thieves climb out to find an empty box, and run away, and Tenali and his wife laugh.
check: Made gentle: Softened for ages 3-9: no threat of stealing or violence shown; the box holds only stones, the thieves are not trapped, beaten, or handed to harsh punishment, they just do silly hard work watering the garden and run away.

outline:
On a hot summer day, a thirsty crow flies far looking for water.
He sees an earthen pitcher in a courtyard garden.
He flies down happily, but finds only a little water deep at the bottom.
He tries to tip the pitcher and stretches his beak, but cannot reach the water.
He looks around and sees small pebbles scattered nearby.
He has a clever idea and drops the pebbles one by one into the pitcher.
The water slowly rises to the top.
The crow drinks the cool water, feels happy, and flies away.
check: Made gentle: This tale is already gentle with no killing or cruelty. Only softened the crow's suffering from thirst to feeling hot and tired, suitable for ages 3-9.

Chiu and Kau, the sparrow and the crow
outline:
Chiu the sparrow builds a little house of wax, and Kau the crow builds a house of cow dung.
The rain comes and washes Kau's house away.
Wet and cold, Kau knocks on Chiu's door and asks to come in.
Chiu says, wait, I am bathing my baby.
Kau knocks again; Chiu says, wait, I am feeding my baby.
Kau knocks once more; Chiu says, wait, I am putting my baby to sleep.
At last Chiu opens the door and gives Kau a warm place by the stove.
The rain stops, and the two friends share a snack together.
check: Drafted from the common telling; the ending is softened (no burning). Change it to how your family tells it.

outline:
A happy monkey lived alone in a big jamun tree by the river, eating sweet purple fruits every day.
A crocodile swam by, and the monkey shared fruits with him, and they became close friends.
The crocodile carried sweet jamun fruits home every day to his wife on the other bank.
The crocodile's wife grew jealous and said she was ill and must have the monkey's heart.
Sad and confused, the crocodile invited his friend the monkey for a visit and carried him on his back across the river.
Mid-river the crocodile confessed his wife's plan, and the monkey quickly thought of a clever trick.
The monkey said monkeys keep their hearts safely on the tree, so they must go back to fetch it, and the crocodile turned back.
The monkey jumped up safely to his tree and told the crocodile their friendship was over.
check: Made gentle: Softened for ages 3-9: the wife's demand for the monkey's heart is kept as in the traditional Panchatantra tale but without any killing, eating, blood, or cruelty shown; it is told as a selfish wish and an unkind trick, and the focus is on the monkey's calm, clever escape to his tree with no harm to anyone.
